children: The Supreme Court on Thursday set aside the write-down of Yes Bank’s Additional Tier-1 (AT1) bonds worth Rs 8,415 crore, providing relief to institutional and retail bondholders whose investments were wiped out during the lender’s 2020 reconstruction. A Bench comprising Justices Dipankar Datta and Augustine George Masih upheld the Bombay High Court’s January 2023 judgment quashing the bond write-down. The apex court dismissed appeals filed by Yes Bank, the Reserve Bank of India and the Centre against the High Court ruling.

The verdict comes nearly five months after the Supreme Court reserved its judgment on May 20 following arguments from the government, RBI, Yes Bank and bondholders. Yes Bank shares fell sharply following the ruling, declining as much as 7.8 per cent intraday to Rs 19.55 apiece.
Dispute Dates Back To Yes Bank’s 2020 Rescue

The case originated from the financial crisis at Yes Bank in March 2020, when rising bad loans and weakening depositor confidence prompted regulatory intervention. The RBI superseded the lender’s board and imposed a moratorium, following which the government approved a reconstruction scheme supported by capital infusion from a State Bank of India-led consortium.

As part of the rescue process, the bank’s administrator wrote down AT1 bonds worth Rs 8,415 crore to zero. AT1 bonds are perpetual debt instruments designed to absorb losses when a bank’s capital falls below specified regulatory thresholds. The legal dispute centred on whether the write-down was permitted under the final reconstruction scheme or could independently be carried out under RBI regulations and the contractual terms governing the bonds.

During proceedings, the Supreme Court examined when a bank should legally be considered reconstructed under Section 45 of the Banking Regulation Act and whether the non-viability trigger permitting an AT1 write-down could operate independently of a completed reconstruction. The Centre maintained that AT1 bonds were governed by RBI regulations and contractual provisions rather than the reconstruction scheme. It also argued that writing down the instruments before the SBI-led capital infusion was necessary to avoid jeopardising the rescue.

Bondholders argued that while provisions concerning the AT1 bonds had been considered in the draft reconstruction scheme, they were omitted from the final scheme. They maintained that the administrator therefore could not subsequently write down the bonds after the scheme came into effect.

The government had also pointed to nearly Rs 1 lakh crore of AT1 bonds outstanding across the banking system and warned about the potential implications of the case for investor confidence and future bank resolutions.

Yes Bank had earlier said that any financial liability resulting from the Supreme Court's decision would be recognised in the relevant future reporting period. The lender had maintained that it did not expect a material financial impact.
